definition: Penurious means extremely unwilling to spend money.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word penurious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know penurious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Our penurious landlord swapped the lobby bulbs for ones so dim that reading the mail required a flashlight.
Thrifty stops far short of penurious — thrift is sensible saving and a virtue.
Tightfisted stops short of penurious — the tightfisted hate opening the wallet, while the penurious act as if it were padlocked.

Miserly means hoarding money for its own sake — the miser loves the pile and suffers to keep it whole. Penurious describes the same shut wallet as a way of life: an extreme unwillingness to spend, whatever the motive behind it. The miserly cherish the hoard; the penurious simply refuse to open it.

Stingy means giving or spending less than a situation fairly calls for — skimping on the tip, the portion, the heating. Penurious goes further and hardens it into character: the penurious refuse to spend at all, as a settled way of life. Stingy shortchanges an occasion; penurious padlocks the wallet.

The memoir opens in penury, with the family pawning the stove to pay winter rent.
Penurious means extremely unwilling to spend money.

Aunt Verna, penurious to the bone, re-wrapped every present she received for future re-giving, logged the household's rubber bands in a ledger, and counted exact bus fare from a jar labeled 'fare, not tips.'
Penurious describes the grip on the purse, not the size of it—an impecunious person has no money to spend, while a penurious one may be rich and still refuse to spend a cent.
It is stinginess worn as a way of life.
Penurious condemns refusal to spend — the padlocked wallet.
'Thrifty' and 'frugal' praise the same instinct in sensible amounts, so choose by verdict.
And keep the unit's money pair straight: impecunious means the money is missing; penurious means the willingness is.

By the time reporters profiled him, Elias Crane owned four freighters and one suit.
The suit was twenty years old.
His office chair had been rescued from a curb, and he wrote memos on the backs of old manifests.
The company's accounts were fat, and Crane could have refitted the whole building without borrowing a cent.
It was, his biographer wrote, something stranger: a penurious streak so settled that spending itself felt to him like injury, whatever the sum and whoever the beneficiary.
When the city asked him to fund a single park bench bearing his name, he declined — then walked home to save the streetcar fare.
